chapter.name: Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'

questions.q: Which national organisation carried out the massive 'People of India' project described in the chapter?
questions.a: The Anthropological Survey of India
o: The Anthropological Survey of India
The Archaeological Survey of India
The Geological Survey of India
The Botanical Survey of India

questions.q: India has over 1.4 billion inhabitants. According to the chapter, about what share of the world's population is this?
questions.a: About 18 percent of the world's population
o: About 18 percent
About 14 percent
About 25 percent
About 1.4 percent

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The historian Vincent Smith wondered how a history of India could be written.
Reason (R): He found India's diversity 'bewildering'.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: Smith asked how, 'in the face of such bewildering diversity', a history of India could be written.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: The People of India project surveyed communities across all States of India. (a) How many communities did it survey? (b) How many languages did it count, and in how many scripts were they written?
questions.a: (a) 4,635 communities. (b) 325 languages, using 25 scripts.
s: States that the project surveyed 4,635 communities
States that it counted 325 languages using 25 scripts

questions.q: Read this line quoted in the chapter: 'How, in the face of such bewildering diversity, can a history of India be written? ... The answer to the query is found in the fact that India offers unity in diversity.' (a) Who wrote it, and what was he? (b) About how long ago did he write it, according to the chapter? (c) In your own words, what answer did he give to his own question?
questions.a: (a) Vincent Smith, a British historian. (b) Over a century ago. (c) That India's history can be written because, beneath all its many differences, India has an underlying unity: it offers unity in diversity.
s: Names Vincent Smith and says he was a British historian
States that he wrote it over a century ago
Explains in own words that beneath India's differences there is an underlying unity (unity in diversity)

questions.q: The chapter opens with Rabindranath Tagore's prayer for 'the touch of the one in the play of the many' and Sri Aurobindo's phrase 'the Many in the One', and later quotes Vincent Smith's answer that 'India offers unity in diversity'. Which idea do all three share?
questions.a: A single underlying unity beneath India's many differences
o: A single underlying unity beneath India's many differences
India's differences make its history impossible to write
India must give up its differences in order to become one
India's variety comes mainly from people moving away from home

questions.q: Which of these puts the two sources in the chapter's opening section in the correct time order?
questions.a: Vincent Smith's question came first, over a century ago; the People of India survey came later, in the late 20th century.
o: Vincent Smith asked his question first; the People of India survey came later, in the late 20th century
The People of India survey came first; Vincent Smith later wrote about its findings
Vincent Smith's question and the People of India survey both belong to the late 20th century
Vincent Smith asked his question while he was directing the People of India survey

questions.q:
Pooja's notes on the opening section of the chapter read:
Line 1: 'The People of India survey was carried out in the early 20th century.'
Line 2: 'Vincent Smith, a British historian, wrote about India's diversity over a century ago.'
Line 3: 'The survey counted 325 languages using 25 scripts.'
Line 4: 'The survey covered 4,635 communities in a few chosen States.'
For each line, say whether it matches the chapter, and correct any line that does not.
questions.a: Line 1 does not match: the survey was carried out in the late 20th century. Line 2 matches the chapter. Line 3 matches the chapter. Line 4 does not match: the 4,635 communities were surveyed across all States of the country, not a few chosen ones.
s: Line 1: says it is wrong and corrects 'early' to the late 20th century
Line 2: says it matches the chapter
Line 3: says it matches the chapter
Line 4: says it is wrong and corrects it to communities across all States

questions.q: Use only these People of India figures from the chapter: 4,635 communities, 325 languages, 25 scripts. (a) On average, about how many communities are there for each language? (b) On average, about how many communities are there for each script? (c) What do your answers to (a) and (b) suggest about how languages and scripts link India's many communities?
questions.a: (a) 4,635 / 325 = about 14 communities per language. (b) 4,635 / 25 = about 185 communities per script. (c) Many different communities share each language, and even more share each script, so a language or a script is a common thread joining many communities: there is some unity even inside this great diversity.
s: Divides 4,635 by 325 to get about 14 communities per language
Divides 4,635 by 25 to get about 185 communities per script
Concludes that many communities share each language and still more share each script, a link (unity) within the diversity

questions.q: Two groups are making a wall chart on 'Unity in diversity' from the chapter's opening pages. Group X wants to show only the People of India figures (4,635 communities, 325 languages, 25 scripts, many Indians who are migrants). Group Y wants to show only the opening lines of Tagore and Sri Aurobindo and Vincent Smith's answer. Evaluate both plans: say what each shows well, what each leaves out, and which you would choose or how you would combine them, with a reason.
questions.a: Plan X shows, with real numbers, how great India's diversity is (communities, languages, scripts, migrants), but it says nothing about the unity beneath that diversity. Plan Y shows the idea of unity in diversity, 'the one in the play of the many' and 'the Many in the One', but gives no evidence of how diverse India actually is. Neither alone shows 'unity in diversity'. The best chart combines them: the figures for the diversity and the quotations for the unity underlying it, which is how the chapter itself opens.
s: States that Plan X shows the size of India's diversity through the survey's numbers
Points out that Plan X leaves out the idea of an underlying unity
States that Plan Y shows the idea of unity in diversity, the one within the many
Points out that Plan Y gives no evidence of how great the diversity is
Makes a reasoned choice, for example combining both because the theme needs both the diversity and the unity beneath it

questions.a: Jowar (sorghum)
o: Jowar (sorghum)

questions.q: Why does the chapter call cereals, millets and pulses 'staple grains'?
questions.a: Because they are the basic food for most Indians
o: They are the basic food for most Indians

They are eaten only on festival days

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B, as given in the chapter.
Column A: 1. Bajra  2. Jowar  3. Ragi  4. Cumin
Column B: P. Sorghum  Q. A spice used throughout the country  R. Pearl millet  S. Finger millet
questions.a: 1-R (bajra is pearl millet), 2-P (jowar is sorghum), 3-S (ragi is finger millet), 4-Q (cumin is a spice used throughout the country)

questions.q: (a) Name the three groups into which the chapter sorts India's staple grains. (b) Give one example from each group.
questions.a: (a) Cereals, millets and pulses. (b) For example: cereal - rice, wheat or barley; millet - bajra (pearl millet), jowar (sorghum) or ragi (finger millet); pulse - a dal or a gram.
s: Names the three groups: cereals, millets and pulses
Gives one correct example for each of the three groups

questions.q: A student is making a five-row chart called 'One plate, many regions' for her classroom. Using the chapter, fill in each row: (a) one cereal common to almost every part of India; (b) one millet, with its other name; (c) one kind of pulse; (d) one spice used throughout the country; (e) one sentence explaining how the same ingredients can give an endless variety of dishes.
questions.a: (a) Rice, wheat or barley. (b) Bajra (pearl millet), jowar (sorghum) or ragi (finger millet). (c) Any dal or gram. (d) Turmeric, cumin, cardamom or ginger. (e) The same basic ingredients (the unity) are used in many different combinations (the diversity), so they give thousands of different dishes.
s: (a) Names a cereal: rice, wheat or barley
(b) Names a millet with its other name, e.g. ragi (finger millet)
(c) Names a pulse: a dal or a gram
(d) Names a spice: turmeric, cumin, cardamom or ginger
(e) Explains that the same ingredients combined in different ways give many dishes (unity and diversity)

questions.q: True or False? 'In the chapter, dals and grams are counted among India's staple grains, along with cereals and millets.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter lists cereals, millets and pulses such as various kinds of dals and grams, and then says 'All these are called staple grains' because they are the basic food for most Indians.
s: Gives the verdict True
Reason: the chapter lists pulses (dals and grams) with cereals and millets and calls all of them staple grains

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Ragi is one of the staple grains named in the chapter.
Reason (R): Ragi is a cereal, like rice and wheat.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the chapter names ragi (finger millet) as a millet, not a cereal, though it is still a staple grain.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: The chapter finds unity in Indian food in the ingredients used across the country. Which finding, if it were true, would most weaken this example?
questions.a: Each region cooked only with grains and spices that no other region used
o: Each region cooked only with grains and spices that no other region used
Each region made its own dishes from rice, dals and turmeric
Some regions used more cumin in their dishes than others did
The number of different dishes in India ran into lakhs

questions.q: Three families in three different States each cook a different flatbread for dinner. Family 1 uses ragi flour with ginger. Family 2 uses bajra flour with turmeric and ginger. Family 3 uses jowar flour with cumin and ginger. (a) Name the ingredient used by all three families, and say which of the chapter's lists it belongs to. (b) Into which group of staple grains do ragi, bajra and jowar all fall? (c) Explain how these three dinners together show both unity and diversity.
questions.a: (a) Ginger; it is one of the spices the chapter says are used throughout the country. (b) Millets. (c) Unity: all three use a millet from the chapter's list of staple grains and a common spice, ginger. Diversity: each uses a different millet and a different mix of spices, so the same kind of ingredients give three different flatbreads.
s: (a) Names ginger and places it among the spices used throughout the country
(b) States that ragi, bajra and jowar are millets
(c) Explains unity (same groups of ingredients) and diversity (different combinations, different dishes)

questions.q:
A community kitchen at Nagpur railway station feeds travellers from many States. Its register for one week (7 days) shows on how many days each ingredient was used: rice 5, wheat 6, jowar 2, moong dal 4, chana dal 3, turmeric 7, cumin 7, cardamom 1.
(a) Which item in the register is a millet, according to the chapter?
(b) Which two spices were used on every day of the week?
(c) How many of the eight items are pulses, and which cereal was used on more days?
(d) Next week the kitchen can stock only four of these items. Which four would you choose so that travellers from most parts of India find the food familiar? Justify using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Jowar (sorghum). (b) Turmeric and cumin. (c) Two pulses (moong dal and chana dal); wheat was used on more days (6, against 5 for rice). (d) For example rice or wheat, one dal, turmeric and cumin: cereals and pulses are staple grains, the basic food for most Indians, and turmeric and cumin are among the spices used throughout the country, so most travellers would know them. Another choice is accepted if it is justified from the chapter's lists of staple grains and common spices.
s: (a) Identifies jowar as the millet
(b) Names turmeric and cumin (used on all 7 days)
(c) States two pulses and that wheat (6 days) was used more than rice (5 days)
(d) Chooses four items and justifies them as staple grains and common spices used across India

questions.a: Paithani
o: Paithani

questions.q: Several travellers to India in past centuries marvelled at the sari. Which qualities of the sari does the chapter say they admired?

Its careful stitching, tight fit and one fixed style

questions.q: True or False? 'According to the chapter, the sari is a fairly new dress in India.' Give the verdict and a reason.

s: Gives the verdict False
Reason: the Vaishali stone relief of a woman in a sari goes back a few centuries BCE, so the sari has a long history

questions.q: (a) What was chintz, according to the chapter? (b) Which two countries decided to ban the import of chintz from India? (c) Why did they ban it?
questions.a: (a) A beautiful type of printed cotton from India that became very popular in 17th-century Europe. (b) England and France. (c) To protect their own products: chintz was so popular that the sale of some European dresses had dropped sharply.
s: (a) Says chintz was a type of printed Indian cotton popular in 17th-century Europe
(b) Names England and France
(c) Explains the ban was to protect their own products, as sales of some European dresses had dropped sharply

questions.q: (a) Name the three kinds of fabric the chapter says saris are made from. (b) The chapter gives two signs that the sari is still changing today: one about its fabric and one about the way it is worn. State both.
questions.a: (a) Cotton, silk and, nowadays, synthetic fabrics. (b) Fabric: saris are nowadays made from synthetic fabrics too. Wearing: new ways of draping the sari are still being invented.
s: (a) Names cotton, silk and synthetic fabrics
(b) States both signs: synthetic fabrics nowadays, and new ways of draping still being invented

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The sari comes in hundreds of varieties.
Reason (R): Women often put the sari to many uses beyond that of a dress.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the varieties come from different fabrics, methods of weaving and designing, and colours; the many uses of the sari are a separate point.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

Read these statements about the sari.
I. The chapter says new ways of draping the sari are still being invented.
II. The chapter says travellers to India found the sari costly and difficult to wear.
III. The chapter says women often put the sari to many uses beyond that of a dress.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: travellers marvelled at the sari's simplicity and economy.
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
A handloom fair in Bhubaneswar has six sari stalls. Stall 1: Banarasi silk with a pattern woven into the cloth. Stall 2: cotton saris with designs block-printed after weaving. Stall 3: Kanjivaram silk with woven borders. Stall 4: synthetic saris with printed flowers. Stall 5: plain Muga silk. Stall 6: cotton saris with woven checks.
(a) Which stalls sell a type of silk sari that the chapter names?
(b) At which stalls was the design added after the cloth was woven?
(c) How many different kinds of fabric are on sale, and what are they?
(d) There is room for one more stall. Option P: a seventh stall of silk saris (Paithani). Option Q: a stall showing different ways of draping one and the same sari. Which would add more to showing the sari's unity and diversity? Justify using your answers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Stalls 1, 3 and 5 (Banarasi, Kanjivaram and Muga). (b) Stalls 2 and 4, where the designs are printed after weaving. (c) Three: silk, cotton and synthetic. (d) Option Q: the fair already shows three silk stalls, three fabrics and both woven and printed designs, but nothing about draping; the chapter says the sari is worn in many ways that vary by region and community, with new ways still invented, yet it remains a single dress, so Q adds a new kind of diversity while showing the unity. (A reasoned case for P, e.g. that it adds another named silk type, earns credit only if it weighs what the fair already shows.)
s: (a) Identifies stalls 1, 3 and 5
(b) Identifies stalls 2 and 4 (printed after weaving)
(c) States three fabrics: silk, cotton and synthetic
(d) Chooses with a reason that weighs what is already shown against draping as diversity within one dress

questions.q: Kunal argues: "'Sari' is just one word for hundreds of completely different dresses. They are made of different fabrics, in different ways, and worn differently, so the sari cannot show any unity." Analyse his argument using the chapter: set out what is right in it, what it misses, and give your verdict.
questions.a: Right: saris come in hundreds of varieties; they are made of cotton, silk (Banarasi, Kanjivaram, Paithani, Patan Patola, Muga, Mysore) or synthetic fabric; by different methods of weaving and designing (some designs woven in, others printed), in endless colours; and are draped in ways that vary by region and community. Missed: every sari is the same plain, unstitched length of cloth worn in most parts of India, and the chapter says 'in the end, it is a single dress'; it has also been worn for a very long time, as the Vaishali relief of a few centuries BCE shows. Verdict: the argument is only half right; the sari shows diversity within a single, shared dress, which is unity in diversity.
s: Accepts the variety of fabrics, including named silk types
Accepts the variety of weaving, designing (woven or printed) and colours
Accepts the variety of draping by region and community
Points out what is missed: one plain unstitched length of cloth worn across most of India, 'a single dress', with a long history (Vaishali relief)
Verdict: the argument is half right; the sari shows diversity within unity

questions.a: False. The map shows the different names of similar festivals held across India about the same date, on or around January 14, when Makara Sankranti marks the start of the harvest season.

Assertion (A): There is an immense variety of festivals in India.
Reason (R): Makara Sankranti marks the beginning of the harvest season in many parts of India.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: R describes one festival; it does not explain why India has so many festivals.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: Farhan claims: 'Makara Sankranti goes by so many names, such as Pongal, Uttarayan and Magh Bihu, so it shows only India's diversity, not its unity.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The many regional names do show diversity. But the chapter shows that these are similar festivals marking the same occasion, the beginning of the harvest season, celebrated across India about the same date (around January 14): that is the unity. So the festival shows both: unity in diversity, not diversity only.
s: Accepts that the many names show diversity
Shows the unity: the same occasion (start of harvest) at about the same date across India
Verdict: partly right; the festival shows unity in diversity, not diversity alone

questions.q:
On 14 January a radio station in Delhi asks listeners from different States what they are celebrating that day. Twelve callers get through. Their answers: Pongal 3, Uttarayan 2, Magh Bihu 2, Maghi/Lohri 2, Makar Sankranti 2, Pedda Panduga 1.
(a) Going by the chapter, what occasion are all twelve callers marking?
(b) How many different names did the callers use?
(c) Which name was used most often, and what fraction of the callers used it?
(d) For its evening programme the station must choose one title: 'Twelve callers, six festivals' or 'One harvest, six names'. Which fits the chapter's idea better? Justify, and say what the other title gets right.
questions.a: (a) The beginning of the harvest season (Makara Sankranti and the similar festivals held about the same date). (b) Six names. (c) Pongal, used by 3 of the 12 callers, that is one quarter. (d) 'One harvest, six names' fits better: the chapter treats these as similar festivals marking the same occasion at about the same date, with different regional names, which is unity in diversity. The other title rightly notices the variety of names (the diversity), but by calling them six separate festivals it misses the unity.
s: (a) States the beginning of the harvest season (Makara Sankranti and its similar festivals)
(b) Counts six different names
(c) Names Pongal and gives 3 out of 12, i.e. one quarter
(d) Chooses with a reason (same occasion, same date, different names) and says the other title captures only the diversity

questions.q: Compare Makara Sankranti and the sari as examples of 'unity in diversity' in the chapter. (a) For each example, state what is the 'one' and what is the 'many'. (b) The chapter supports the festival example with a map and the sari example with a stone relief. Analyse what each kind of evidence shows. (c) Conclude what the two examples together suggest about Indian culture.
questions.a: (a) Festival: the one is a single occasion, the beginning of the harvest season around January 14; the many are its regional names (Pongal, Uttarayan, Magh Bihu, Maghi/Lohri and others). Sari: the one is a single dress, a plain unstitched length of cloth worn in most of India; the many are its fabrics, weaves, designs, colours and ways of draping. (b) The map shows the festival spread across the country at the same time; the Vaishali relief, a few centuries BCE old, shows the sari has lasted over a very long time. (c) Together they suggest that Indian culture celebrates diversity as an enrichment but never loses sight of the unity underlying it; diversity does not divide, it enriches.
s: Festival: one occasion (start of harvest, about January 14) and many regional names
Sari: one unstitched dress and many fabrics, weaves, designs, colours and drapes
Map evidence: the festival spread across India at about the same date
Relief evidence: the sari's long history, back to a few centuries BCE
Conclusion: Indian culture celebrates diversity as enrichment without losing the underlying unity

questions.q: Make a four-box flow chart for a class wall that traces the journey of the Panchatantra as the chapter describes it. Box 1: where it began (its language and its age). Box 2: how it spread within India. Box 3: where it travelled beyond India and what it inspired there. Box 4: the result today, with the chapter's estimate.
questions.a: Box 1: an original Sanskrit text, at least 2,200 years old. Box 2: its stories were adapted in almost every Indian language. Box 3: they travelled to Southeast Asia, the Arab world and Europe, inspiring new collections of stories on the way. Box 4: about 200 adaptations exist in more than 50 languages: one collection has become many.

Box 2: adapted in almost every Indian language

questions.q: (a) Name the three regions beyond India to which the Panchatantra's stories travelled. (b) The chapter says the stories inspired 'new collections of stories on the way'. Why does this make the Panchatantra an especially good example of 'one' becoming 'many'?
questions.a: (a) Southeast Asia, the Arab world and Europe. (b) Because the single original collection did not only get copied or translated; it gave rise to new and different collections in other lands, so one source became many different works.

III. Its stories stayed within Asia and never reached Europe.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only. II is wrong: the two epics are the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. III is wrong: the stories travelled to Southeast Asia, the Arab world and Europe.
o: I only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only

questions.q: Which of these would NOT count as one of the Panchatantra's 'many', as the chapter uses the idea?
questions.a: A Sanskrit poem about the Pandavas fighting to recover their kingdom
o: A Sanskrit poem about the Pandavas fighting to recover their kingdom
A Telugu retelling of its animal stories that teach life skills
A new Arabic collection of animal stories inspired by its tales
A European book of fables drawn from its old Sanskrit stories

questions.q: The Panchatantra is discussed in the chapter's section 'An Epic Spread', yet it is not an epic. (a) What is an epic, according to the chapter? (b) Why does the Panchatantra not fit this meaning? (c) What does it share with the two epics that earns it a place in this section?
questions.a: (a) A long poem generally narrating the adventures of heroes and other great figures of the past. (b) The Panchatantra is a collection of stories whose main characters are animals and which teach life skills; it does not narrate the adventures of heroes. (c) Like the epics, it began as a Sanskrit text and spread into many adaptations in many languages, in India and beyond, so it too shows literature as unity in diversity, one becoming many.
s: (a) Gives the chapter's meaning of epic: a long poem narrating the adventures of heroes and great figures of the past
(b) Explains that the Panchatantra is a collection of animal stories teaching life skills, not a narrative of heroes
(c) Identifies the shared feature: a Sanskrit original that spread into many adaptations (one becoming many)

questions.q:
At a book fair in Guwahati, one stall shows only books linked to the Panchatantra. It has 8 books: an edition of the original text; retellings in Assamese, Hindi, Bengali and Tamil; a Thai picture book printed in Bangkok, Thailand; an Arabic collection of fables inspired by it; and an English translation printed in London.
(a) In which language is the edition of the original text written?
(b) How many of the 8 books show the stories travelling beyond India, and to which region named in the chapter does each belong?
(c) The chapter estimates that about 200 adaptations exist. What percentage of that estimate does the stall hold, if the original edition is not counted?
(d) A visitor says the stall is far too small to show 'one becoming many'. Do you agree? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Sanskrit. (b) Three: the Thai picture book (Southeast Asia), the Arabic collection (the Arab world) and the English translation printed in London (Europe). (c) 7 adaptations out of about 200 = 3.5%. (d) Partly: the stall holds only about 3.5% of the estimated adaptations, so it cannot show the full scale; but even this small sample shows one Sanskrit source in 8 books and 8 languages, spread across India and to all three regions beyond India the chapter names, so it does show one becoming many. A reasoned verdict either way is accepted if it uses both the percentage and the spread.
s: (a) States Sanskrit
(b) Counts 3 and places them in Southeast Asia, the Arab world and Europe
(c) Computes 7/200 = 3.5%
(d) Gives a verdict that weighs the small share (3.5%) against the spread across languages and regions

questions.q:
A Class 6 group from Coimbatore goes on a nature walk in a forest of the Nilgiris. Their guide stops at a small shrine around a carved stone and says: 'This stone is called Pancha Pandavar. It shows five brothers. My community, the Irula, looks after this shrine because, our elders say, these brothers once passed through this forest.'
(a) Which five brothers does the stone show?
(b) To which epic do they belong?
(c) Besides the brothers themselves, name one other figure from that epic whom tribal legends, according to the chapter, sometimes say visited their region.
(d) Which observation by the anthropologist K.S. Singh does this shrine fit? Explain in one line.
questions.a: (a) The five Pandava brothers. (b) The Mahabharata. (c) Draupadi, the Pandavas' wife, or Duryodhana, their cousin and adversary. (d) K.S. Singh observed that there is hardly a place in the country which the epic heroes such as the Pandavas did not visit according to folklore; the Irula shrine is one such local legend of the Pandavas passing through.
s: (a) Identifies the five Pandava brothers
(b) Names the Mahabharata
(c) Names Draupadi or Duryodhana
(d) Links the shrine to K.S. Singh's remark that the Pandavas, according to folklore, visited almost every place in India

questions.q: True or False? 'According to the chapter, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata became known across India mainly through people reading the original Sanskrit texts.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. The epics spread through translations and adaptations into regional literatures, countless folk versions and tribal versions passed on orally; Nehru found them widely known among the masses in popular translations and paraphrases, with even illiterate villagers knowing hundreds of verses by heart.

Reason: they spread through regional translations, folk and oral tribal versions, and popular translations known even to illiterate villagers

questions.q: (a) What did the anthropologist K.S. Singh observe about the places the Pandavas visited, according to folklore? (b) What did Jawaharlal Nehru find about how ordinary villagers knew the epics, on his travels before Independence? (c) Using (a) and (b), explain why the chapter calls the epics 'another example of unity in diversity'.
questions.a: (a) That there is hardly a place in the country which the epic heroes such as the Pandavas did not visit, according to folklore. (b) That the epics were widely known among the masses through popular translations and paraphrases; even illiterate villagers knew hundreds of verses by heart and filled their talk with references to them. (c) The same two stories (unity) are known all over India, but each place keeps them in its own languages, local legends and versions (diversity), creating a dense web of cultural interactions across India.
s: (a) States K.S. Singh's observation that the Pandavas visited almost every place according to folklore
(b) States Nehru's finding that the epics were known even to illiterate villagers through popular translations and paraphrases
(c) Explains the same stories (unity) known everywhere in many local forms (diversity)

questions.q: Shreya argues: 'The many folk and tribal versions of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata prove that Indians do not share one culture, because every community tells the stories differently.' Evaluate her argument using the chapter: give the evidence that supports the first part, the evidence she has overlooked, and your verdict.
questions.a: Supports: there are countless folk versions (about a hundred Mahabharata versions in Tamil Nadu alone); the Bhils, Gonds, Mundas and most tribes of the northeast and Himalayan regions have their own versions; communities keep legends linking the heroes (the Pandavas, Draupadi, sometimes Duryodhana) to their own region, like the Irula shrine in the Nilgiris. Overlooked: all these are versions of the same two epics with the same core stories (the Pandavas recovering their kingdom; Rama defeating Ravana); K.S. Singh noted that folklore takes the heroes to almost every place in India; the epics created a dense web of cultural interactions across India and Asia. Verdict: the argument is wrong; the different versions are diversity within a shared story, which the chapter calls unity in diversity: diversity does not divide, it enriches.
s: Gives evidence of many versions: about a hundred Mahabharata folk versions in Tamil Nadu, tribal versions of the Bhils, Gonds, Mundas and others
Notes local legends linking epic heroes to the tribes' own regions, e.g. the Irula shrine
Points out that all are versions of the same two epics with the same core stories
Uses K.S. Singh's remark or the 'dense web of cultural interactions' to show a shared culture
Verdict: the argument fails; the versions are diversity within a shared story (unity in diversity)
